3801.lemma: ὁ ὢν καί ὁ ἦν καί ὁ ἐρχόμενος
3801.translit: ho ṑn kaí ho ēn kaí ho erchómenos
why: ὁ ὢν καί ὁ ἦν καί ὁ ἐρχόμενος does not occur in the Byzantine (Majority) New Testament text.
No Byzantine NT occurrences; evidence comes from other corpora and lexica only.

prose.def: A fixed three-part divine title in Revelation meaning 'the one who is, who was, and who is coming,' expressing God's eternal existence across all time.
prose.article: This isn't a single word but a fixed phrase used as a divine title, stitching together "the one being" (present participle of εἰμί), "the one who was" (its imperfect), and "the one coming" (present participle of ἔρχομαι). Strong's frames it as a name for the Eternal, applied as an epithet of Christ. The construction is striking because it freezes verb forms into noun-like titles, treating God's existence across past, present, and future as a name rather than a description.
prose.caution: There are no measured occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament corpus, and the lexical evidence cited (Abbott-Smith) covers only the ordinary verb "to be," not this phrase as a whole, so its sense rests on the construction itself rather than corpus measurement.

issues: Definition assumes 'is to come' (future) as the third element, but the Greek uses the present participle ἐρχόμενος ('the one coming'), which the KJV glosses variously as 'art to come' or 'shalt be' — the definition should flag this distinction

The entry has zero corpus occurrences in the Byzantine NT, so all definitional claims rest on compositional analysis and Strong's, not measured usage; this methodological limitation is noted in the caution but not reflected in the confidence of the definition itself
Abbott-Smith evidence covers only εἰμί as a general verb and does not attest the compound divine title as a lexical unit; the definition over-relies on it

Strong's attributes the epithet specifically to Christ, but the phrase in Revelation is also applied to God the Father (e.g., Rev 1:8, 4:8), making 'applied as an epithet of Christ' an oversimplification

No specific NT verses are cited in the supporting article to anchor the definition, since corpus occurrence count is 0 — the entry should more prominently direct readers to the Revelation passages where the phrase appears in critical texts

receipts.how: The threefold title appears in the greeting of Revelation applied to God, demonstrating the phrase functions as a fixed divine name in the critical text even though it registers zero occurrences in the Byzantine corpus counted here.
The living creatures use the same threefold formula in worship, showing the title is a repeated liturgical epithet in Revelation rather than a one-off construction.
The phrase is spoken by 'the Lord God, the Almighty,' confirming the title is applied to God the Father and not exclusively to Christ, which the current definition's Strong's citation obscures.

audit.author_note: The phrase is exclusive to the Revelation of John in the NT critical text; no Pauline, Lukan, or other authorial usage exists, so the definition's context is entirely apocalyptic and doxological — readers of other NT books will not encounter it.

prose.def: To ensnare or entrap someone, used figuratively in the NT of opponents plotting to catch Jesus out with a question.
prose.article: Pagideúō means to ensnare or trap someone, used figuratively rather than for literal hunting. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 22:15, where opponents plot to trap Jesus 'in his words' (ἐν λόγῳ). The Septuagint uses it twice to render Hebrew terms for snaring or being caught, and Moulton-Milligan note a striking parallel in the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, where someone looks for a way 'to trap me' — confirming this was ordinary Koine vocabulary for laying a snare.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint, so the measured range rests on a single verse.

classical.lsj: πᾰγιδ-εύω , ( παγίς ) lay a snare for, entrap , LXX 1 Ki. 28.9 , Ev.Matt. 22.15 .

issues: The measured syntactic role is listed as 'vocative (1×)', which is unexpected for a verb and likely a data artifact, but the definition does not address or account for this anomaly

The sense label 'out conspired trap' is awkward corpus metadata, not a clean lexical label; the existing label 'to trap with words' is narrower than the classical lexicons (Dodson: ensnare, entrap, entangle) which do not restrict it to words

The phrase 'especially with words' in the definition over-specifies from the single NT example (ἐν λόγῳ in MAT 22:15) and could mislead readers into thinking the word inherently means verbal trapping, when the broader lexical sense is simply 'to ensnare/entrap'
Abbott-Smith's LXX references (1Ki 28:9 and Ecc 9:12) suggest a literal or non-verbal snaring context in at least one use, undermining the 'especially with words' qualifier

receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence shows opponents plotting to trap Jesus 'in his word' (ἐν λόγῳ), which supports the figurative sense but also shows the 'with words' qualifier is a contextual modifier, not inherent to the verb itself
The verb takes an accusative object (Jesus) with the instrumental phrase ἐν λόγῳ added separately, confirming that verbal trapping is the circumstance here, not the core lexical meaning of the verb

As the only NT occurrence, this verse both validates and limits the definition: it demonstrates the figurative ensnaring sense but cannot alone establish 'with words' as the word's defining characteristic

prose.def: A trap or snare, used figuratively in the NT for a hidden spiritual or moral danger that ensnares someone, especially the devil's trap.
prose.article: παγίς is a trap or snare — originally a device for catching birds — and the New Testament uses it both literally and figuratively for a hidden danger that springs on someone unaware. The Byzantine NT has it 5 times, and although the rendering tool lists "dwell" and "become" as separate senses, those reflect how surrounding phrases were translated rather than different meanings of the word itself; the core sense throughout is "snare." It's heavily attested in the Septuagint (51 times), most often translating the Hebrew פָּח (a fowler's trap, 13 times), and it even turns up in a fifth-century Christian epitaph where the deceased boasts of escaping "the grievous nets and mournful snares of sin."
prose.caution: The "dwell" and "become" senses are artifacts of phrase-level translation, not real distinct meanings, so the word effectively has a single sense: snare.

receipts.how: Paul quotes Psalm 69 calling Israel's table a 'snare,' clearly demonstrating the figurative trap/snare sense the definition centers on.
The verse speaks of escaping 'the snare of the devil,' directly confirming the figurative hidden-danger sense in the definition.
The rendering 'dwell' diverges from the snare sense, illustrating where the definition fails to account for a measured 20% of occurrences.

audit.author_note: Paul uses παγίς consistently for diabolical or social traps in theological argument (ROM 11:9, 1TI 3:7, 1TI 6:9, 2TI 2:26), while Luke's single use (LUK 21:35) occurs in an eschatological warning with a rendering divergent enough that readers of Luke may not recognize the word's core snare meaning without qualification.

prose.def: Something one undergoes or experiences: (1) suffering or affliction, especially hardship endured; (2) a passive emotion, passion, or inner drive.
senseLabels: an enduring of suffering (verbal-noun sense, with object)
passions or emotions (inner drives or affections)
prose.article: πάθημα refers to something one undergoes — most often hardship or suffering. In the Byzantine NT it is rendered "sufferings" 8 times (50%) and "suffering" 4 times (25%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% on both. The lexicons add a notable extra range the corpus counts barely capture: it can also mean a passive emotion or passion (Abbott-Smith cites Galatians 5:24 and Romans 7:5), and Moulton-Milligan notes the word was originally fairly colorless — a disposition or propensity — before drifting toward the sense of evil experience or suffering.
prose.caution: The measured NT senses center on "suffering," but the lexicons document a distinct "passion/emotion" sense that the raw rendering counts underrepresent.

issues: The definition treats the 'passion/emotion' sense as merely secondary or occasional, but it is attested in at least two distinct Pauline texts (GAL 5:24, ROM 7:5) and the lexicons give it full parity as a second major sense—the current wording ('sometimes an inner emotion or passion') undersells this.

Sense label 2 ('an undergoing of suffering') is nearly identical to sense label 1 and fails to distinguish the 'passion/emotion/affection' sense documented by Abbott-Smith, Strong's, Dodson, and KJV ('affection', 'motion'), which deserves its own label.

The definition's phrasing 'something a person undergoes' is accurate for senses 1 and 3 but awkward for sense 2 (passive emotion/passion), where the word describes an internal disposition or drive rather than an external experience endured.
The rare rendering 'belong' and the KJV gloss 'motion' are not accounted for at all, leaving the 'disposition/propensity' nuance documented in Moulton-Milligan unaddressed.

receipts.how: Demonstrates the dominant 'sufferings' sense clearly: 'the sufferings of Christ overflow to us,' confirming the word's primary use for external hardship endured.

Abbott-Smith and Moulton-Milligan cite this verse for the 'passion/emotion' sense ('passions and desires'), showing the word can denote internal drives rather than experienced affliction—a sense the current definition only weakly acknowledges.

Abbott-Smith lists this as the 'an enduring or suffering' sense with a genitive object ('the suffering of death'), illustrating the verbal-noun nuance that sense label 2 attempts but fails to distinguish clearly.

audit.author_note: Paul (Romans, Galatians) uses the word for internal passions or emotions (ROM 7:5, GAL 5:24), while Peter, Hebrews, and Paul's other letters use it almost exclusively for external suffering or affliction—readers of Galatians or Romans may be misled by a definition that foregrounds suffering alone.

prose.def: Describing Christ as one who was capable of, subject to, or destined to suffer — the precise nuance is disputed among sources.
senseLabels: capable of / subject to / destined to suffer
prose.article: παθητός is a verbal adjective from the same root as πάθημα (suffering), and it appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 26:23, where it describes the Christ as one destined to suffer. The Majority Standard Bible renders the single occurrence in the phrase "suffer rise," agreeing fully with the Berean Standard Bible. Notably, Moulton-Milligan points out that this is the only verbal adjective ending in -τός in the whole New Testament, and Abbott-Smith records two possible nuances: "one who has suffered" or "subject to suffering."
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources differ on whether it means "having suffered," "capable of suffering," or "destined to suffer."

prose.def: An ungoverned, passive emotion or depraved passion; in every NT occurrence a sinful passion or lust.
prose.article: πάθος refers to a violent, ungoverned emotion or passionate desire, and in all three of its New Testament appearances it carries a negative meaning — a sinful passion or lust. The word's root sense is actually "that which one suffers," something that happens to you, and you can see that passive flavor in how it differs from ἐπιθυμία, the more active and comprehensive word for desire. Interestingly, the everyday papyri show the same range: one first-century BC document speaks of someone acting "from his own passion," while another inscription uses the plural to invoke "all the evils and sufferings" that befall people as a curse on tomb-robbers.
prose.caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the sense labels reflect translation choices in specific phrases rather than three distinct meanings.

issues: Sense label 2 ('earthly (sinful) impulse') is a mistranslation artifact: COL 3:5 lists 'πάθος' in a vice list where 'earthly' modifies the whole list, not πάθος itself; the word still means 'passion/lust' there

receipts.how: 'πάθη ἀτιμίας' (passions of dishonor) confirms the word means ungoverned passion in a clearly negative sense, supporting the core definition.
'πάθει ἐπιθυμίας' shows πάθος paired with ἐπιθυμίας to form a compound phrase; the label 'lustful craving' wrongly collapses both words into πάθος alone.
πάθος appears in a vice list where 'earthly' is a list-level modifier, not a gloss for πάθος itself, exposing the mislabeling of sense 2.

audit.author_note: Paul uses πάθος in all three NT occurrences across Romans, Colossians, and 1 Thessalonians, always in vice-list or ethical-warning contexts, so no cross-author variation is detectable.

prose.def: A trusted household slave who supervised boys' conduct — used figuratively by Paul for the Law's temporary, guiding role pointing to Christ, now ended for believers.
senseLabels: guardian or supervising attendant (figurative: Law as guide to Christ, 1CO 4:15; GAL 3:24)
guardian or supervising attendant (same role, GAL 3:24 parallel)
no longer under a guardian (termination of the Law's supervisory role, GAL 3:25)
prose.article: A παιδαγωγός was a household slave charged with escorting boys and overseeing their behavior and morals — not a teacher in the strict sense, as Abbott-Smith notes by distinguishing him from the διδάσκαλος. The word appears 3 times in the New Testament across 2 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "guardian" (the two GAL 3:25 and 1CO 4:15 phrases counted separately are really the same single sense). An everyday papyrus letter (P Oxy VI.930) captures the role perfectly: a mother urges her son and his παιδαγωγός to find a suitable teacher, then sends greetings to "your highly esteemed attendant Eros" — showing the close, affectionate place such an attendant often held.
prose.caution: Confidence is low: only 3 occurrences, and the three "measured senses" are really one meaning split by translation phrasing.

receipts.how: Demonstrates the figurative theological sense: the Law functions as a παιδαγωγός 'leading to Christ,' showing the word is used allegorically, not just literally.
Shows where the definition needs qualification: the παιδαγωγός relationship is declared ended ('we are no longer under a guardian'), a negative/termination sense the definition ignores.
Abbott-Smith notes this as the antithesis of πατήρ, confirming the non-teacher, supervisory sense the definition captures, but also the figurative application Paul favors.

audit.author_note: Both NT authors using this word are Paul, but within Galatians he uses it both positively (the Law as guide toward Christ, 3:24) and negatively (the supervisory role now ended, 3:25), a dialectical tension the definition should flag.

prose.def: A young boy or lad, originally a diminutive form but sometimes used more loosely for older youths.
prose.article: παιδάριον is a small-form version of παῖς (child) and basically means a young boy or lad. In the New Testament it appears just once, in John 6:9, describing the boy with the loaves and fish, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "boy" every time. What's interesting is that the diminutive sense often faded in everyday Koine: papyri and inscriptions use it for everything from an unborn child to, in Tobit 6:2-3, a young man strong enough to haul a fish ashore. In the Septuagint it appears 206 times, most often translating the Hebrew na'ar (158×), a word for a young man or servant.
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and evidence that its diminutive force was often lost, the precise age it implies in any given passage is uncertain.

prose.def: The process of forming a person through training and corrective discipline, as from a parent or God, encompassing instruction, moral education, and redemptive chastening.
senseLabels: endurance of hardship as divine discipline
prose.article: παιδεία covers the whole process of forming a person—training, education, and the corrective discipline that goes with it. In the Byzantine New Testament its six uses lean toward "discipline" (4 of 6, 67%), with "instruction" once and disciplined suffering once, while classical lexica note it could also simply mean rearing or schooling a child. The Septuagint uses it 57 times, most often (32×) for the Hebrew מוּסָר, the word for moral correction, and the papyri confirm its everyday sense of education "befitting freeborn children."
prose.caution: With only six New Testament occurrences, the balance between "correction" and broader "training" depends heavily on context, and the lexica stress the wider educational range more than the measured NT usage.

prose.def: A teacher or instructor who trains others; in Hebrews, extended to one who corrects or disciplines, as a father or God.
prose.article: παιδευτής describes someone who instructs and trains, coming from the verb παιδεύω. It appears only twice in the New Testament: once rendered "instructor" (Romans 2:20), and once absorbed into the phrasing rather than a single English word. The lexicons stretch the range a bit wider than the measured data: Abbott-Smith and Dodson note a second sense, "a corrector" or "one who disciplines" (as in Hebrews 12:9), and the word's only Septuagint use translates a Hebrew word tied to discipline. The papyri show it as an ordinary term for a paid teacher, as in an inscription about wages owed to teachers.
prose.caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the disciplinary sense rests on the lexicons rather than the measured renderings, so treat the range as tentative.

prose.def: To educate, train, or bring up a person, ranging from teaching and instruction to disciplining or punishing them.
senseLabels: to teach, instruct, or bring up
prose.article: παιδεύω covers a spectrum from gentle instruction to firm correction, all rooted in raising and shaping a person. In the Byzantine New Testament the Majority Standard Bible renders it "disciplined" 5 times (71%) and "punish" twice (29%), with another 6 of its 13 occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The classical lexicons add a milder educational side—Abbott-Smith notes the "train, teach, instruct" sense in passages like Acts 7:22—while the everyday papyri show both: one prodigal's appeal to his mother reads "chastened I have been as I deserve," and another describes someone "educated in every kind of learning." In the Septuagint it appears 58 times, most often translating the Hebrew יָסַר ("to discipline"), 30 times.
prose.caution: The measured New Testament data shows only the "discipline" and "punish" senses, while the lexicons also list a milder "teach/instruct" sense not captured in these counts.

prose.def: An adverb meaning 'from childhood' or 'from infancy,' marking the starting point of a condition or behavior that has continued since a person was young.
prose.article: παιδιόθεν is an adverb formed from παιδίον ("child") with the ending -θεν that signals source, so it literally means "from childhood." It appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 9:21, where it is paired with the preposition ἐκ; the classical equivalent was the phrase ἐκ παιδός. The word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Moulton-Milligan compares the parallel formation ἐξ οἰκόθεν ("from home") in a first-century document.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its meaning rests on very thin biblical evidence, though the papyri and classical sources agree.

prose.def: A female slave, servant girl, or young woman; in Galatians also used allegorically of Hagar as a type of the law-covenant.
senseLabels: slave woman (allegorical, of the Sinai covenant)
prose.article: παιδίσκη is the feminine diminutive of παῖς ("child") and most often means a female slave or servant girl, the sense in about 42% of its 13 New Testament occurrences, with another 17% rendered simply "girl." In Galatians 4 it appears twice as "woman," referring to Hagar the slave woman, and the Septuagint uses it 76 times to translate the Hebrew words for maidservant (שִׁפְחָה 35×, אָמָה 29×). Moulton-Milligan note that the word originally meant just a young woman but came in later Koine to denote a female slave, a shift confirmed by everyday papyri where παιδίσκη is bought and sold like property.

It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Corinthians 10:7), where it describes the festive revelry around the golden calf, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "indulge revelry" every time. In the Septuagint it shows up 23 times, usually translating the Hebrew שָׂחַק ("to laugh, sport," 11×), and a sepulchral inscription captures its lighter sense vividly: "play, indulge, live—you must die."
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise New Testament shade rests heavily on the Old Testament quotation it appears in.

It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 23:18, where the entire crowd cries out together against Jesus, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "unison" while older versions say "all at once." Built from the words for "all" (πᾶς) and "multitude" (πλῆθος), it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and a related form appears in Aristeas describing a "vast accumulation" of sacrificial blood.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning rests on limited evidence.

prose.def: An adjective meaning very great or very much, describing something extremely large in amount or number.
prose.article: πάμπολυς is a compound of "all" (πᾶς) and "much" (πολύς), meaning "very great" or "very much" — a strong way to describe a huge crowd or quantity. It is well known from classical Greek and everyday Koine papyri, where it describes things like "a great deal of wood" or events "a very long while afterwards." In the Bible it appears only in the Textus Receptus reading of Mark 8:1 (describing a very large crowd); modern critical editions read "again a large crowd" (πάλιν πολλοῦ) instead, so the word may not belong to the New Testament text at all.
prose.caution: This word rests on a single disputed reading in Mark 8:1 that modern critical texts replace, so its New Testament status is uncertain; the measured "became" reflects surrounding phrasing rather than the word's actual meaning.

The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Pamphylia" in every occurrence; the variant phrasings the digest lists ("after in Pamphylia," "after Pamphylia") just reflect surrounding words, not different meanings. prose.def: A public lodging-house where travelers could find shelter for the night.
prose.article: πανδοχεῖον refers to a public lodging-place — what we might call an inn, khan, or caravanserai — where travelers could stop and be taken in. Its parts literally suggest a place that "receives all," and the word was everyday colloquial Koine, showing up in comic writers and ordinary papyri and inscriptions. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:34, where the Good Samaritan brings the wounded man to an inn; related papyri even use a form for the innkeeper's trade.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on outside evidence rather than biblical usage.

prose.def: A solemn or festive public assembly, especially a grand national or religious gathering held in honor of a deity or occasion.
prose.article: πανήγυρις describes a grand festive assembly — originally a national gathering held in honor of a god, but used more broadly for any joyful public celebration. It appears just once in the New Testament (Hebrews 12:23), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "joyful," capturing the celebratory mood. In the Septuagint it shows up 4 times across 3 books, usually translating the Hebrew word חָג ("festival," 3×), and the papyri show it was a common everyday word for festivals and public meetings — at Fayum it even appears alongside markets, marking a clear festal occasion.

prose.def: An adverb (Byzantine text only) meaning 'with one's whole household,' describing an action done together by an entire family or domestic group.
prose.article: πανοικί is an adverb formed from "all" (πᾶς) and "house" (οἶκος), describing something done together with one's whole family or household. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 16:34, where the Philippian jailer rejoices along with everyone in his home. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri: this word was a stock phrase in the closing greetings of private letters, where writers regularly wished a friend well "with all the household" (e.g. a second-century letter prays for someone to be in good health πανοικεὶ).
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and ancient sources disagree on the spelling and form (Abbott-Smith notes strict Atticists rejected it and preferred the form -κίᾳ).

prose.def: A soldier's complete set of weapons and protective gear—the full equipment for battle.
prose.article: πανοπλία refers to a soldier's entire battle kit, both defensive armor and weapons—the word combines πᾶς ("all") with ὅπλον ("weapon/equipment"). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, rendered "armor" twice (67%) and "full armor" once (33%), and Paul famously applies it metaphorically to "the full armor of God" in Ephesians 6:11 and 13. prose.def: Clever, unscrupulous shrewdness employed for deceptive or manipulative ends; in the NT always used negatively of cunning trickery or craftiness.
prose.article: πανουργία describes the kind of shrewdness that gets used for deception — cunning, trickery, or sly maneuvering. In the New Testament it appears 5 times and almost always carries a bad sense; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "cunning" in two-thirds of cases (as in 2 Corinthians 11:3 and Ephesians 4:14), and elsewhere folds it into phrasing like Jesus seeing through their craftiness in Luke 20:23. prose.def: An adjective meaning crafty or cunning (usually negatively), though in some contexts it can mean simply clever or skilful.

prose.def: From all sides or every direction (and abstractly, 'on all points'); attested in NT only in the Textus Receptus of Mark 1:45, absent from the critical text.
senseLabels: from all sides / from every quarter
prose.article: πανταχόθεν is an adverb meaning "from all sides" or "from every direction," and it's the source-form built on πανταχοῦ ("everywhere"). It's vanishingly rare in the Bible: it appears in only one Byzantine NT verse (the Textus Receptus of Mark 1:45, where crowds came to Jesus from every quarter) and just twice in the Septuagint (4 Maccabees). Here the digest shows a mismatch worth flagging: the Majority Standard Bible's count renders it "openly," while every lexicon (Strong's, KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) and the papyri agree the word means "from all sides." Moulton-Milligan shows it was common in everyday Koine papyri, as in a third-century letter advising someone to "get together all you can" to buy a good tunic.
prose.caution: The single measured rendering ("openly") conflicts with every cited lexicon, which gives "from all sides," and the word appears in only one disputed NT verse, so treat the sense data with caution.

prose.def: An adverb meaning 'everywhere' or 'in all places,' modifying verbs to indicate that an action or condition extends to every location.

prose.article: πανταχοῦ simply means "everywhere" or "in all places," and the measured senses really just reflect different sentence contexts—sometimes paired with "people" or with words of opposition—rather than separate meanings. It appears 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "everywhere" in 4 of those (57%), with the others being variations on the same idea. The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite papyri like a B.C. 248 letter saying "we have looked for wood everywhere," and legal documents declaring an agreement valid "everywhere."
prose.caution: In Acts 21:28 the form is actually πανταχῇ (a spelling variant), which some editors prefer, so that occurrence is grouped here under the same word.

The most interesting clue comes from the papyri: a property sale dated A.D. 212 uses the same phrase to mean "from now on forever," suggesting the Hebrews passage may carry a time sense — to save "finally" or permanently — which fits the "always lives" idea right after it.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and both inside one fixed phrase, whether it means "completely" or "forever" in Hebrews 7:25 is genuinely disputed.

prose.def: An adverb meaning 'in every way' or 'entirely,' used once in the NT to intensify a verb, with papyri confirming the sense 'wholly' or 'under all circumstances.'
prose.article: This adverb, built from πᾶς ("all"), means "in every way" or "entirely." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 24:3, where the Majority Standard Bible folds it into the sense of "acknowledge" within Tertullus's flattering speech to Felix. The everyday papyri are especially telling: it regularly pairs with πάντως in the phrase πάντῃ πάντως, meaning "under all circumstances" or "by all means," as in a 311 BC contract and a letter urging "be very sure to send Pindarus."
prose.caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only one measured occurrence, so its range there rests almost entirely on outside evidence from the Septuagint and papyri.

prose.def: An adverb meaning 'from all sides' or 'on every side,' describing spatial coverage or encirclement in every direction.
prose.article: πάντοθεν is an adverb meaning "from all sides" or "on every side," built from πᾶς ("all"). It appears only a handful of times in the New Testament — twice in the Byzantine text, three times in critical editions — typically describing something completely surrounded, as when Jesus warns that enemies will hem Jerusalem in on every side (Luke 19:43). The papyri show it was everyday Koine: a property sale from 88 BC uses it for whatever "adjoins on all sides," and Moulton-Milligan note it replaced the older Attic form πανταχόθεν.
prose.caution: The measured sense labels here ("hem" and "jar") reflect surrounding English phrasing rather than the word's actual meaning, and with so few occurrences the data is thin.

prose.def: A title for God meaning the one who rules and holds power over all things; the Almighty.
prose.article: Pantokrátōr is a divine title meaning "the all-ruling one," rendered "Almighty" in all 10 New Testament occurrences, and nearly all of them appear in Revelation, with the single exception of 2 Corinthians 6:18. It is far more common in the Septuagint, appearing about 150 times, where it most often translates the Hebrew word for "hosts" (צָבָא, 113×) and the divine name Shaddai (15×), giving us phrases like "the LORD Almighty." Interestingly, Hort suggested the title means not simply One who can do anything, but One who holds together and controls all things, and the word is almost unknown outside Jewish and Christian writers — Moulton-Milligan could cite only a single pagan inscription using it.

receipts.how: 'I am the Alpha and the Omega,' says the Lord God, 'who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty (παντοκράτωρ)' — a clear titular use for God as all-ruling sovereign, supporting the core definition.
The sole non-Revelation NT occurrence, quoting an OT formula, 'says the Lord Almighty (παντοκράτωρ)' — confirms the word functions exclusively as a divine title across both NT authors and contexts.
The living creatures cry 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty (παντοκράτωρ),' echoing the LXX Sebaoth liturgy and corroborating the definition's link to the Hebrew 'hosts' background.

audit.author_note: Revelation uses the title nine times in vivid apocalyptic doxologies and judgment scenes, whereas 2 Corinthians 6:18 uses it once in a quiet OT quotation about covenant relationship; the theological weight is the same but the rhetorical register differs markedly.

prose.def: An adverb meaning at every moment or on every occasion; always.
prose.article: πάντοτε is a simple adverb of time built from "all" and "when," meaning "always" or "at all times." Its range is narrow and consistent: of 42 occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "always" 33 times (83%), with the rest being phrasings like "all times" or "time" that carry the same meaning. The word turns up in everyday Koine letters too — one papyrus has a slave writing to her master, "I always pray for your health" (εὔχομαι πάντοτε περὶ τῆς ὑγιείας σου), showing it was common, ordinary language.

prose.def: An adverb meaning 'surely,' 'certainly,' or 'by all means,' used to strengthen affirmations and, with a negative, to make a denial complete or emphatic.
senseLabels: by all means, altogether (expressing totality or intention)
in no wise, by no means (with negative, completing or strengthening denial)
prose.article: πάντως is an adverb built from πᾶς ("all"), and it works to intensify whatever it modifies — "surely," "certainly," or "by all means." It appears 9 times in the Byzantine New Testament, but in 3 of those cases it dissolves into the phrasing without its own English word, which is why translators render it so flexibly. With a negative it sharpens the denial into a complete one (Romans 3:9). The everyday flavor shows up nicely in the papyri, where one writer urges, "Be sure, Aphrodisius, to send me the loaves and the relish."
prose.caution: The measured renderings split evenly between "surely" and "all," and a third of occurrences carry no English word of their own, so the exact force depends heavily on context.

prose.def: A preposition meaning 'beside' or 'near' whose sense—'from' (genitive), 'with/at' (dative), or 'alongside/beyond' (accusative)—is determined by the case it governs.

was present with (dative in existential clause)
from with / received from (blended genitive phrase)
from such a person (genitive, demonstrative context)
any at all (accusative, comparative or conditional frame)
with a / in the presence of (dative with article)
prose.article: παρά is one of Greek's hardest-working prepositions, built on the core idea of "beside" or "near," but its English rendering depends heavily on the grammar and context. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 200 times, most often translated "from" (34%) when marking a source or origin, and "with" (20%) when describing being alongside a person; remarkably, 87 of those 200 occurrences carry no English word of their own and are simply absorbed into the phrasing. One striking detail: in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew word for "sign" (אוֹת) 97 times, the most frequent of its Hebrew counterparts, showing how loosely a preposition can map across languages.
prose.caution: Because παρά changes meaning with the case it governs and is often swallowed into English phrasing, no single gloss captures it—readers should weigh each context separately.

prose.def: To transgress or violate a command or tradition; or, with ἀπό, to turn aside and fall away from a rightful position or role.
senseLabels: turn aside / fall away from a position
prose.article: At its core παραβαίνω means to step over a line — to break a command, rule, or tradition you were meant to keep. The Byzantine New Testament uses it only 4 times, three of them clearly about violating commands or traditions (as in Matthew 15:2–3), with one occurrence in Acts 1:25 describing Judas turning aside and abandoning his rightful position. The Septuagint employs it 37 times, often rendering the Hebrew סוּר ("to turn aside") and פָּרַר ("to break"), and Greek classical authors like Homer used it literally for standing beside before it took on its dominant metaphorical sense; everyday papyri also use it for transgressing oaths and contracts.
prose.caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and the Acts 1:25 "turn aside" sense differing from the more common "transgress," the precise range in a given verse can be debated.

prose.def: To compare things side by side, or (reflexively, of travelers/ships) to arrive at or put in at a place; a middle-voice form also risks one's life.
prose.article: παραβάλλω literally means to throw one thing beside another, and from that root it branches into two main uses: comparing things side by side, and (of seamen) putting in or touching at a place. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice, and in both cases it was absorbed into the phrasing rather than translated as a single English word. The everyday papyri back up the travel sense nicely—one letter from the 3rd century BC scolds a man who 'passed us by' instead of landing to visit for even a quarter of an hour, matching the rendering 'we touched at Samos' in Acts 20:15.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament occurrences (one in the critical text), both absorbed into phrasing—so the senses rest mainly on Septuagint, papyri, and classical attestation.

prose.def: The violation of an explicit law or command — crossing a boundary established by a formal standard, whether deliberate or not.
prose.article: παράβασις means a transgression—deliberately crossing a line that a law or command has drawn. The Majority Standard Bible renders all 5 visible occurrences as "transgression" (the other 2 of its 7 New Testament uses are absorbed into surrounding phrasing), and it is closely tied to its verb παραβαίνω, "to step across." Interestingly, the classical lexicon Abbott-Smith notes an older sense of simply "a going aside, a deviation," while everyday Koine papyri use the word for the breach or violation of a contract or agreement, complete with stated penalties.
prose.caution: The word appears only once in the Septuagint and just 7 times in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on relatively thin evidence.

prose.def: A person who transgresses or breaks a law, especially the law of God; consistently used in the New Testament alongside 'of the law' (νόμου).

All five New Testament uses point to this single idea, often paired with "of the law" (νόμου) in Romans and James, so the word's range is narrow and consistent. Interestingly, the older lexicon Abbott-Smith records a literal first sense — "one who stands beside," the warrior riding alongside the charioteer — but that physical meaning never appears in the New Testament, which uses only the moral "transgressor" sense.
prose.caution: The word appears just 5 times, and the four measured renderings vary in wording, though they all converge on the same basic meaning of "lawbreaker."

prose.def: To press or compel someone by insistent entreaty, carrying an undertone of forceful constraint, until they comply.
prose.article: παραβιάζομαι describes pressing someone hard with entreaties until they yield, and in both of its New Testament appearances it has this sense of insistent persuasion — as when the disciples 'urged' Jesus to stay with them in Luke 24:29. prose.def: A comparison, illustrative story, or symbolic figure used to convey a deeper truth; in the Synoptics almost always a teaching parable of Jesus, in Hebrews a symbolic type or figure.
senseLabels: a short proverbial or rhetorical comparison
prose.article: παραβολή literally means setting one thing beside another, and across its 50 New Testament uses it almost always points to the vivid comparisons and illustrative stories—parables—found in the synoptic Gospels, rendered "parable" or a variation 81% of the time. In the Septuagint it usually stands in for the Hebrew מָשָׁל (25 times), a word that covers proverbs and sayings as well as comparisons, which is why the classical lexica also list senses like "proverb," "figure," and "analogy" (for example in Hebrews 9:9 and 11:19). The most telling detail is that Hebrew background: the same term that gives us "parable" also produced the broader "adage" or "figure" range the NT only occasionally uses.

prose.def: To expose oneself to danger or risk one's life (or, in the Received Text variant παραβουλεύομαι, to disregard one's own safety).
senseLabels: exposing oneself to danger / risking one's life (critical text); disregarding one's safety (Received Text variant)
prose.article: This rare word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Philippians 2:30, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "disregarding" — describing someone who set aside concern for his own life. There's a textual wrinkle: many editions read the closely related form παραβολεύομαι, which means "to expose oneself to danger" or "hazard one's life." The most telling evidence comes from an Olbian inscription of the second century AD, cited by Deissmann, where this very word describes a man who "risked" dangers for friendship's sake all the way to the ends of the earth — proof it was ordinary Koine, not a coinage of the NT author.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin and the sources disagree: this is a once-occurring word with a disputed spelling, and "disregard" versus "risk oneself" hinge on which textual form is read.

prose.def: A command, charge, or directive given by someone in authority, ranging from official orders to apostolic or pastoral instructions.
prose.article: παραγγελία is an authoritative directive — an order, charge, or instruction handed down by someone with standing to give it. The five New Testament uses cluster tightly around this idea, rendered as "orders," "instructions," or "instruction," whether it's the Sanhedrin's command not to teach (Acts 5:28) or the apostle's charge to believers (1 Thessalonians 4:2). The everyday papyri sharpen the picture: one document (P Oxy 1411, A.D. 260) warns that those who disobey "this injunction" will face penalties, and the word could even mean a formal summons to appear in court — and classical writers like Xenophon and Polybius used it specifically for a military order.
prose.caution: With only five occurrences, the boundaries between the measured senses are subtle and rest on thin evidence.

prose.def: To transmit an authoritative directive—to command, instruct, or formally charge someone, often through a chain of authority.
prose.article: παραγγέλλω means to hand down an authoritative instruction, ranging from a firm command to a solemn charge; the Majority Standard Bible spreads its 30 occurrences across "instructed" (5×), "command" (5×), "ordered" (3×), and "give" (2×), with 11 more absorbed into surrounding phrasing. Built from παρά plus the root of ἄγγελος ("messenger"), its core idea is transmitting a message that carries weight. Moulton-Milligan shows the most telling background: in Ptolemaic papyri the word commonly describes an official court summons—calling someone to appear before authority—which matches its consistently authoritative tone in the New Testament.
prose.caution: The senses cluster tightly around "command/order," but with no single dominant rendering and a third of occurrences blended into phrasing, exact shades depend heavily on context.

prose.def: To come, arrive, or appear at a place; occasionally, to stand by or support someone (2 Tim 4:16).
prose.article: παραγίνομαι is a movement verb meaning to arrive, come, or show up somewhere, and across its 37 Byzantine occurrences the renderings cluster tightly around "came" (12×) and "arrived" (10×), with a few framed as "when" someone arrived and a few as "went." It works as a near-synonym for the ordinary verb "to come" (ἔρχομαι), and Moulton-Milligan notes a scholar overstated things by calling it a "choicer" word than the plain alternative. In the Septuagint it appears 124 times, most often translating the Hebrew בּוֹא ("to come/go," 14×), and the older lexicons preserve an additional sense "to stand by, support someone" (as in 2 Timothy 4:16) that the measured New Testament renderings don't otherwise capture.
prose.caution: The classical lexica list a "stand by, support" sense not reflected in the measured renderings, so its full range is slightly broader than the corpus data alone suggests.

The Byzantine NT has it 10 times, and where it gets its own English word the Majority Standard Bible renders it "passing" in 3 of those cases, with the BSB agreeing entirely; in 3 of 10 occurrences it simply blends into the surrounding phrasing. Interestingly, papyri show a transitive sense "bring forward" that the NT never uses — one document (BGU IV.1139) even uses it of compelling a man to produce his daughter. prose.article: παραδειγματίζω means to expose someone to public shame, putting them on display as a humiliating example. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (once in the critical text), and in both cases English translations fold it into the surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own word. The Septuagint uses it 5 times, and outside the Bible Plutarch uses it of the poet Archilochus making himself infamous through his verses, while everyday papyri show the related noun simply meaning "example."

prose.def: A heavenly realm or garden of blessing, used in the New Testament for God's presence or reward for the faithful, entered by the dead or in visionary experience.

prose.article: The word originally meant a garden or enclosed park, and in everyday Koine papyri it very commonly refers to an orchard of fruit-trees, usually walled. The Greek Old Testament uses it 27 times, mostly to render the Hebrew word for "garden" (20×), including the garden of Eden in Genesis. In the New Testament, however, all three occurrences point to Paradise as the dwelling place of the blessed dead, as in Jesus' promise on the cross (Luke 23:43). Interestingly, the word is a foreign borrowing of Iranian origin, related to the modern Persian word for garden.
prose.caution: Confidence is low: there are only 3 New Testament occurrences, and the everyday "garden/park" meaning seen in the Septuagint and papyri does not appear in the New Testament's spiritual usage.

prose.def: Ongoing mutual friction or irritation arising from useless disputes, especially among people who are corrupt in mind and deprived of truth.
prose.article: This rare word describes ongoing, fruitless disputes that breed mutual irritation, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Timothy 6:5). The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "constant," describing the endless friction stirred up by quarrelsome people, and older sources cast it as "useless wrangling" or "perverse disputing." Notably, the critical text reads a slightly different form (διαπαρατριβαί), which Field connects to the idea of "mutual irritations," comparing the simpler word παρατριβαί used by Polybius for tensions between Carthaginians and Romans.
prose.caution: This word rests on thin evidence, appearing only once and only in some minuscule manuscripts, with the critical text preferring a different spelling, so its exact form and force are disputed.

prose.article: παρακαθίζω simply means to sit down next to someone. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 10:39, where Mary sits beside Jesus to listen, and the critical text doesn't use this exact form at all. Notably, the same word shows up in the Septuagint at Job 2:13, where Job's friends sit beside him, and Moulton-Milligan find the related forms in everyday papyri and inscriptions, including one phrase about "sitting in on the lectures."
prose.caution: Evidence is thin: just one disputed New Testament occurrence (replaced by παρακαθέζομαι in critical texts) and one Septuagint use, so confidence is low.

prose.def: To urge, encourage, comfort, or earnestly beg someone, depending on context; occasionally to summon or invite someone for a purpose.
prose.article: παρακαλέω literally means to call someone near, and from that base it spreads across a warm range of meanings: it can urge (28×, 40%), encourage or console (20×, 29%), or beg and plead (18×, 26%). Which sense applies depends entirely on context — whether you are exhorting a friend, comforting the grieving, or desperately pleading for help. The Septuagint mostly uses it for the Hebrew נָחַם, "to comfort," and the papyri show it as a stock polite phrase in everyday private letters ("I ask and beg you to take care of the child"), confirming how ordinary and personal the word felt.
prose.caution: The senses shade into one another, and 38 of 108 occurrences are absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own, so the boundaries between urging, encouraging, and begging are often a translator's judgment call.

prose.def: To hide or conceal something, literally by placing a covering beside it, or figuratively of something kept from understanding.
prose.article: παρακαλύπτω literally means to cover something by hanging a screen beside it, and by extension to veil or conceal. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 9:45, where it is folded into the phrasing rather than given its own English word — there the meaning of Jesus' saying was "concealed" from the disciples. The Septuagint uses it twice, where it renders Hebrew words for being hidden or dismayed, and Moulton-Milligan notes the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, pushing back against Grimm's suggestion that its Lukan use is a Hebraism.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint — and the Hebrew counterparts cited differ between sources.

prose.def: Something entrusted for safekeeping, especially the body of apostolic teaching committed to a believer's faithful guard (Pastoral Epistles, Textus Receptus).
prose.article: παρακαταθήκη refers to something handed over to another for safekeeping — a deposit or entrusted possession. The word doesn't appear in the Byzantine New Testament, but it shows up twice in the Septuagint (in one book) and was the more usual form in Greek writers, often replacing the variant παραθήκη in some New Testament textual traditions. Everyday papyri richly illustrate its commercial flavor: one third-century document (P Oxy I.71) speaks of "a secure deposit, subject to no claim or charge," showing it was the ordinary word for a legally protected entrusted sum.
prose.caution: This word does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament and appears only twice in the Septuagint, so its biblical sense rests on thin attestation and the related form παραθήκη.

prose.def: To be present or lie close at hand; used of something (the will, a principle) that is near or available to a person.
senseLabels: present / at hand (of the will to do good)

prose.article: παράκειμαι literally means to lie beside something, hence to be near, present, or ready at hand. It shows up only twice in the New Testament, both in Romans 7 (verses 18 and 21), where translators render it differently — once as something being 'present' or available ('discover'), and once as a 'principle' that is always close by. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same down-to-earth way: one son writes to his mother that if more money 'had been at hand' he would have sent it (P Oxy III.530).
prose.caution: Confidence is low: with only two New Testament uses, both in the same chapter, the word's full range is thinly attested and translators handle the two cases quite differently.

prose.def: Encouragement, comfort, or consolation that strengthens someone; also exhortation or an earnest appeal, depending on context.
prose.article: This word covers a cluster of closely related meanings centered on coming alongside someone to strengthen them—whether through encouragement, comfort, or consolation. In the Byzantine New Testament, the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'encouragement' 7 times (29%) and 'comfort' 6 times (25%), with the rest shading between these, so the two ideas blend together rather than splitting apart. The Septuagint shows the comfort side clearly, where it 4 times translates the Hebrew tanchumim ('consolations'); the everyday papyri, however, often carry the more transactional sense of an 'appeal' or 'entreaty,' as in a documented request to let soldiers travel.
prose.caution: The classical lexica list a fourth sense—'appeal' or 'entreaty'—that barely surfaces in the measured New Testament data, so its full range is broader than the rendered senses alone suggest.

prose.def: A helper called alongside to aid another, functioning as an advocate or intercessor before God and as a comforter or helper in the believer's life.
senseLabels: advocate with the sense of active help or benefit to the recipient
prose.article: παράκλητος literally describes someone "called alongside" to help, and in legal settings means an advocate or pleader who speaks on another's behalf. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Advocate" in all 5 New Testament occurrences (one as "Advocate" expressing benefit), and the term appears only in John's writings, applied to the Holy Spirit (John 14:16, 26; 16:7) and to Christ (1 John 2:1). Notably, the King James Version translated it "comforter," and Strong's and Dodson add the sense of consoler or helper—so older sources stretch the word toward comfort while the measured renderings favor the courtroom idea of an advocate; the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri.
prose.caution: Sources disagree on range: measured renderings consistently give "Advocate," but older lexica (KJV, Strong's, Dodson) also list "comforter/consoler," and the word occurs only 5 times.
